title: The Second Cup
text:
Daniel had been drinking four cups of coffee a day for six years. He did not think it was a problem until his doctor asked a simple question: "How well do you sleep?"

He could not answer. He fell asleep late, woke early, and felt tired all day. The doctor did not tell him to stop. She only {{1}} that he keep his last cup before two o'clock.

The first week was hard. By four in the afternoon his head hurt and he wanted to give up. But he noticed something in the second week. He was falling asleep before midnight.

He still drinks coffee. He just stops earlier. Small changes are easier to keep than big ones, and a change you keep is worth more than a change you {{2}}.

glossary.definition: to stop trying to do something
having a certain value or use

clozes.hint: she offered an idea for him to think about

questions.prompt: What did the doctor actually ask Daniel to do?
options: Drink his last coffee before two o'clock
Visit her again in a week
questions.rationale: The text says she did not tell him to stop, only to keep his last cup before two.

questions.prompt: What happened in the second week?
options: He began falling asleep before midnight.
He went back to four cups.
questions.rationale: The third paragraph states he noticed he was falling asleep before midnight.

questions.prompt: What point does the last paragraph make?
options: A change you can keep is more useful than a big change you cannot.
Sleeping early is the only way to feel rested.
questions.rationale: The final sentence compares a change you keep with a change you fail.

title: Why Maps Lie
text:
The Earth is round. A map is flat. You cannot make a round thing flat without changing it, so every world map is wrong in some way. The question is not whether a map lies, but which lie it chooses.

One common map keeps the shapes of countries {{1}} but makes the ones far from the equator look much larger than they are. On that map, Greenland looks about the same size as Africa. In fact Africa is fourteen times larger.

Another map keeps the sizes correct but bends the shapes near the edges. Neither map is better in every case. A sailor and a student do not need the same map.

So when you look at a map, it helps to ask what the mapmaker decided to {{2}}. Every map answers that question, though it rarely says so out loud.

glossary.definition: the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth
to change the shape of something so it is no longer straight

clozes.hint: almost the same as the real shape
to make something smaller or give up some of it

questions.prompt: Why does the writer say every world map is wrong?
options: A round surface cannot be shown flat without change.
questions.rationale: The first paragraph gives the round-to-flat problem as the reason.

questions.prompt: What does the Greenland example show?
options: A map can distort size while keeping shape.
questions.rationale: The map keeps shapes similar but makes distant countries look far larger than they are.

questions.prompt: What does the writer advise readers to do?
options: Ask what the mapmaker chose to give up.
Use only one kind of map.
Avoid maps of the whole world.
questions.rationale: The last paragraph tells readers to ask what the mapmaker decided to reduce.
